# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Does development assistance for education improve learning outcomes? Cross-country panel evidence has been used to answer yes, no, and "it depends," but the field has paid less attention to whether the answer is stable across the methodological choices it conditions on. We assemble a 133-country, 2010–2020 panel from OECD CRS disbursements, World Bank Human Capital Index Harmonized Learning Outcomes (HLO), and the standard macro / governance / sector controls, and we run the brief's pre-specified five-model architecture (cross-section, within-country fixed effects, multilevel, intervention-typology ANOVA, counterfactual simulation) under an *ex ante* commitment design in which every consequential analytical choice is locked in an Architecture Decision Record before its analysis runs. The within-country fixed-effects specification recovers a positive aid-to-learning coefficient (β = +11.14 HLO points per unit log treatment; p ≈ 0.05; N = 143 country-cycles) on the World Bank HCI HLO outcome — the empirical observation cross-country panel evidence at this data shape unambiguously supports. The pre-commitment design, however, surfaces three findings that reshape how to read this result. First, the four-bucket intervention typology the literature treats as policy-relevant (infrastructure / teacher training / curriculum / budget support) is not extractable from CRS project metadata at the inter-method agreement threshold we committed to; the ANOVA does not run. Second, substituting the published AAP-2018 harmonized learning measure for the World Bank HCI HLO measure flips the within-country coefficient's sign in both the full and the overlap-window samples (β = −16.67 and −3.94 respectively); the headline is measure-sensitive. Third, the standard multiple-imputation robustness check the missingness ADR pre-committed to requires assumptions our MCAR test pre-committed to running already refutes. Alongside these, the paper constructs a novel Human Capital × AI Readiness joint composite that quantifies a previously unmeasured ≈2× over-representation of sub-Saharan Africa in the low-HCI ∩ low-AI-readiness cell. We position the paper in the methodological-reflection tradition [@sandefur2018internationally; @vivalt2020generalize; @deaton2018rcts] and read its contribution as *a calibrated map of what cross-country aid-effectiveness panel evidence can and cannot say at the current data frontier*.

# 1. Introduction — The measurement illusion

Universal primary enrollment is, by the standards of any prior era of development policy, a solved problem. Across the 133 ODA-eligible recipient countries in our 2010–2020 panel, gross primary enrollment is uniformly between 98 and 109 percent; the MDG-era convergence on access has reached every region. *Learning* has not converged. Human Capital Index Harmonized Learning Outcomes (HLO) range from roughly 300 to 625 across the same country set, with no narrowing trend across the four HCI cycles published since 2010. The policy literature has, over the same decade, converged on a near-universal lever: redirect education aid away from inputs that the access-era apparatus knows how to deliver (classrooms, enrollment subsidies, teacher headcount) and toward interventions that produce learning — targeted pedagogy, accountability mechanisms, structured-instruction at-scale rollouts [@glewwe2016improving; @geeap2023smart; @angrist2024lays]. The empirical record on whether aid actually moves learning, however, is contested — and the contestation depends as much on methodological choices as on substantive findings.

This paper assembles the canonical cross-country panel the contestation has been conducted on, runs the brief's pre-specified five-model architecture, and operates under a design choice the cross-country aid-effectiveness literature has not historically committed to: *every consequential analytical decision is locked in writing in an Architecture Decision Record before the analysis whose result the decision would influence runs*. The decision record names the options considered, the criterion that would distinguish them, and the threshold at which the criterion would be considered met. When the analysis subsequently runs, the criterion either is or is not met; the record makes the outcome auditable and the response disciplined. The brief's Three-Pass Self-Review Protocol — statistical validity before any writing, argumentative coherence after the full draft, adversarial read after a 48-hour gap — adds a second tier of pre-commitment around the manuscript itself.

The within-country panel fixed-effects specification, which is the cleanest identification claim this kind of data supports, recovers a positive aid-to-learning coefficient: β = +11.14 HLO points per unit log of three-year-moving-average constant-USD CRS disbursement, country-clustered SE = 5.52, p ≈ 0.05, N = 143 country-cycles. The cross-sectional specification yields β = −1.36 (non-significant) on the same panel, controlling for the same covariates; the within-country result is the structural empirical claim this data identifies and the contested literature has not consistently delivered. *This single number is not the principal contribution of this paper.* Three pre-committed methodology gates that the paper's brief required us to run surfaced findings that reshape how to read it.

The first gate was the intervention-typology question. The brief specified Model 4 as a one-way ANOVA on a four-bucket typology — infrastructure aid / teacher-training aid / curriculum-materials aid / budget support — coded from OECD CRS project descriptions. Architecture Decision Record 0007 (ADR-0007) pre-committed to a binding inter-method agreement threshold (raw agreement ≥85 %; Cohen's κ ≥0.70; rule-based unclassified <30 %) between a regex-based classifier and a purpose-code-derived classifier as the gate for using the typology in the ANOVA. All three thresholds failed; the typology cannot be extracted from CRS project metadata at the agreement we committed to. Model 4 was dropped rather than escalated to hand-coding. The second gate was the published-measure robustness check ADR-0004 committed to: refit the within-country coefficient using the Altinok-Angrist-Patrinos (2018) harmonization in place of the World Bank HCI HLO measure, and verify sign agreement. The AAP-2018 coefficient is β = −16.67 on the full AAP sample and β = −3.94 on the year-overlap window restricted to 2010 onward; sign agreement fails. The headline result is real in the World Bank HCI HLO specification but does not generalize across the published learning-harmonization choice. The third gate was the missing-data sensitivity check ADR-0006 pre-committed to: run the multiple-imputation UIS-augmented robustness on the full sample alongside the listwise-complete UIS-augmented spec. The MCAR test ADR-0006 also required came back rejected at p ≪ 10⁻⁶ on every relevant subset; multiple imputation's MAR assumption is therefore not empirically supportable on this data, and ADR-0012 retires the MI sub-commitment in favor of the listwise spec alone.

Alongside these three discipline findings, the paper executes a fourth substantive analysis the brief committed to: a novel joint composite of the World Bank Human Capital Index and the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index 2025, partitioned into median-split quadrants. The empirical finding is that 47 of 132 joined countries (35.6 %) fall in the low-HCI ∩ low-AI-readiness "double-excluded" cell, and 29 of those 47 (61.7 %) are sub-Saharan African — against sub-Saharan Africa's 31.8 % share of the joined sample. The compounding-divergence thesis that UNDP, the World Bank's *Beyond the AI Divide* working paper, and the joint ILO–World Bank background study for the *World Development Report 2026* have articulated theoretically [@muthukrishna2025divergence; @mandon2025beyond; @ilo2026disruption] receives a concrete country-cross-section operationalization with explicit regional-concentration quantification.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. §2 reviews the cross-country aid-effectiveness literature [@burnside2000aid; @easterly2004aid; @glewwe2016improving; @hanushek2008role] and the methodological-reflection strand we position alongside [@sandefur2018internationally; @vivalt2020generalize; @deaton2018rcts; @pritchett2013rebirth]. §3 describes the data sources, the panel construction, the brief's pre-commitment design, and the positionality of practitioner-researcher authorship. §4 reports descriptive patterns and walks the empirical models in the order the discipline arc requires — the Models 1–2–3 chain establishing the within-country positive coefficient, then the Model 4 drop, the Model 5 counterfactual on the locked aggregate β, the Compounding AI Penalty composite, and finally the HLO measure-fragility finding. §5 discusses what the paper as a whole can and cannot claim. §6 draws policy implications. §7 concludes.

# 2. Literature Review

The cross-country aid-effectiveness debate, the education-specific aid-and-learning literature, and the methodological-reflection strand on what empirical-development research can credibly claim are three distinct conversations that this paper sits at the intersection of. We engage each in turn — briefly, since the paper's contribution is the synthesis at the intersection rather than incremental advances within any one strand.

## 2.1 Cross-country aid-effectiveness empirics

The canonical question — *does development aid raise growth?* — has been answered in the affirmative, the negative, and conditionally in the same data over the last two-and-a-half decades. The widely cited finding by Burnside and Dollar [-@burnside2000aid] was that aid raises growth only in countries with good fiscal, monetary, and trade policies; their aid × policy interaction term entered cross-country growth regressions with a positive and significant coefficient on an instrumental-variables design. The conditional-effectiveness finding was widely interpreted as policy advice — *target good-policy countries* — and shaped a generation of aid-allocation debate. Easterly, Levine, and Roodman [-@easterly2004aid] subsequently showed that the Burnside-Dollar interaction does not survive extension of the original sample to more countries and years; the result is fragile to sample composition. The two papers together — and the subsequent extensions in the aid-and-growth-in-Africa GMM literature [@asongu2019aid] — left the field with a robust *methodological* finding even where the substantive coefficient remained contested: interaction-effect claims in cross-country aid-effectiveness panels are sensitive to sample, specification, and the choice of instrument. The lesson is one our pre-commitment design takes seriously: in @sec-methods §3 we specify the within-country fixed-effects specification before estimating it, and we report sample and specification sensitivities in §4 rather than searching across them for the most favorable result.

The cognitive-skills-for-growth strand associated with Hanushek and Woessmann [-@hanushek2008role; -@hanushek2015knowledge] re-framed the same broad question — *what makes education translate into development?* — at the *outcome* level. Cross-country growth regressions using harmonized test-score measures (rather than years of schooling or enrollment) find that cognitive skills explain a substantial share of cross-country income variation that schooling alone does not capture. The implication for aid is direct: if learning is what matters for growth, and aid is meant to support development, then aid that fails to move learning is structurally misaligned with its stated purpose. This paper is the education-aid-specific extension of that logic — taking the cognitive-skills-as-outcome framing as the dependent-variable construction and asking whether the donor-side input (CRS-recorded education-sector ODA) moves the learning-side output (HCI HLO).

## 2.2 Education-specific aid effectiveness

Within education, the field's evidence base on *what aid composition actually produces learning* is broader at the program-evaluation level than at the country-panel level. Glewwe and Muralidharan's [-@glewwe2016improving] *Handbook of the Economics of Education* review synthesizes a substantial RCT and quasi-experimental record on developing-country education interventions and identifies a recurring pattern: pedagogical interventions (targeted instruction; teaching at the right level; structured pedagogy at scale) and accountability mechanisms produce larger learning gains per dollar than mass input interventions (more teachers; more textbooks; more classrooms) in many evaluated settings. The GEEAP "Smart Buys" framework [@geeap2023smart] codifies this into a cost-effectiveness ranking that has shaped donor practice. Angrist and colleagues' Learning-Adjusted Years of Schooling (LAYS) framework [@angrist2024lays] provides a reporting unit that puts micro-cost-effectiveness findings on a scale comparable to country-level outcomes.

The relationship between education *spending* and learning is, in the published cross-country evidence, conditional rather than monotonic. Vegas and Coffin's [-@vegas2015when] analysis using PISA scores and cumulative per-student expenditure data found that the spending–learning relationship plateaus above a threshold (roughly USD 8,000 cumulative spending per student); below the threshold, additional spending raises outcomes; above it, the marginal returns are negligible. Pritchett's [-@pritchett2013rebirth] *The Rebirth of Education: Schooling Ain't Learning* — the closest qualitative intellectual ancestor of this paper — argues that the broader system of education aid and policy has been organized around inputs (enrollment, completion, expenditure) rather than outcomes (what children can actually do) because the input metrics are politically tractable and the outcome metrics are politically inconvenient. The institutional concept Pritchett develops — *isomorphic mimicry*, where education systems adopt the forms of effective schooling without the substance — connects the empirical pattern (input-tracking, learning-stagnating) to the donor-side incentive structures that perpetuate it.

Taken together, these strands give the *program-evaluation* and *spending-threshold* literatures plenty to say about what works in education and where the binding constraints are. They do not, however, give a clean cross-country panel test of *whether the aid that countries actually receive moves their learning outcomes over time* — which is the question the cross-country panel data we assemble is sized to answer, with the limits we own in §4 and §5. The brief's Model 4 design (a four-bucket intervention-typology ANOVA on CRS disbursements) was the planned operationalization of the field's "what aid composition produces learning" question; §4.4 reports the pre-committed protocol failure that prevents Model 4 from running on the available donor-reporting data. That failure is itself a finding for this literature — the pedagogical-vs-input-mass distinction the field treats as policy-load-bearing is *not extractable from CRS metadata at country-year resolution*, and §5 takes that as a methodological contribution rather than as a caveat against the paper's other results.

## 2.3 Methodological-reflection tradition

This paper positions its contribution alongside a small but growing strand in development empirics that treats *what an empirical method can and cannot credibly claim* as itself a methodological contribution — not a caveat to be acknowledged before moving on, but a substantive finding the literature should know about. Sandefur's [-@sandefur2018internationally] *Internationally comparable mathematics scores for fourteen African countries* is the clearest precedent on the outcome-measurement side: it re-analyzes the SACMEQ–PISA item overlap underlying the harmonized learning measures the field treats as cross-country comparable, finds that anchor-sample sizes are often too thin for credible item-equating, and concludes that cross-test rankings rest on harmonization assumptions weaker than the literature has admitted. This paper engages Sandefur head-on in §3, defending the within-country fixed-effects specification as the answer to the level-comparability concern Sandefur raises (within-country variation does not require cross-country score comparability), but accepting that the alternative-harmonization robustness check Sandefur's critique anticipates is exactly the test we report in §4.7 — and on which the headline within-country coefficient does not survive sign-agreement.

On the cross-country-generalizability side, Vivalt's [-@vivalt2020generalize] meta-analysis of impact-evaluation external validity finds that effect sizes in development RCTs vary substantially across contexts — heterogeneity is large enough that single-study estimates routinely do not transport. Deaton and Cartwright [-@deaton2018rcts], in *Understanding and misunderstanding randomized controlled trials*, argue more broadly that the RCT methodological community over-interprets the inferential warrants that randomization itself supports; covariate imbalance, treatment-effect heterogeneity, and the absence of a credible causal model can each undermine the routine "RCT = gold standard" framing. The substantive method Vivalt and Deaton-Cartwright critique (RCTs) differs from the method this paper uses (cross-country panel FE), but the *over-claiming* concern carries: the cross-country-panel community has likewise tended to report a within-FE coefficient as if it were measure-independent, sample-independent, and identification-robust, when in fact each of those properties needs to be tested rather than assumed. The path-c framing of this manuscript — and the §3 pre-commitment design that operationalizes it — places the paper deliberately in this lineage.

The compounding-divergence literature — Muthukrishna and Schellekens' [-@muthukrishna2025divergence] UNDP report, Mandon's [-@mandon2025beyond] *Beyond the AI Divide* World Bank working paper, and the joint ILO–World Bank *Disruption without dividend?* background study [-@ilo2026disruption] for the *World Development Report 2026* — articulates a different methodological-reflection theme. These works argue that AI-driven divergence between countries is conditional on absorptive capacity (human capital, digital infrastructure, governance) and that the standard country-comparison tools have not yet operationalized the joint distribution of those capacities at country-cross-section resolution. The §4.6 Compounding AI Penalty analysis is our contribution at that joint-distribution operationalization layer; we cite the three above as the closest theoretical (Muthukrishna-Schellekens) and practitioner (Mandon; ILO-WBG) antecedents we are aware of, while noting in §4.6 that we are not aware of a prior peer-reviewed paper that constructs the HCI × Oxford-GARI joint composite at the exact country-cross-section level we report.

# 3. Data & Methodology

## 3.1 Data sources and panel construction

The analytical panel is a balanced 133-country × 11-year (2010–2020) dataset assembled from ten administrative and harmonized-research sources. The country universe is the set of recipient countries that received any positive OECD CRS commitment between 1995 and 2024 *and* recorded at least one Human Capital Index Harmonized Learning Outcomes (HLO) observation in the period; 127 of the 133 carry the ≥2 HLO cycles required for within-country slope identification in Model 2. The 2010–2020 primary window is HCI-cycle-anchored — HLO is observed only in 2010, 2017, 2018, and 2020 — so wider windows (2000–2022 and 2005–2020) yield mechanically identical Model-2 samples; both are reported as referee-resistant robustness alongside the primary. COVID-affected years (2020–2022) are handled with a time-varying school-closure control derived from the UNESCO HDX daily-status time series; a parallel robustness drops 2020+ entirely.

The outcome variable is the World Bank Human Capital Index Harmonized Test Scores (`HD.HCI.HLOS`), fetched via the WDI API and stored as `hlo_score` (scale roughly 300–625, anchored on PIRLS/TIMSS primary benchmarks at 400/475/625). The principal robustness measure is the Altinok, Angrist and Patrinos [-@altinok2018global] *Global Data Set on Education Quality (1965–2015)* — a parallel harmonization stored as `aap_hlo_aap` and fetched from the OWID `owid-datasets` GitHub mirror at a frozen commit hash. ADR-0004 commits the paper to verifying sign-agreement on the within-country coefficient across the two measures as a precondition for the headline claim; §4.7 reports the measure-sensitivity finding from that test. The Sandefur [-@sandefur2018internationally] critique that anchor-equating between testing regimes (PISA, TIMSS, SACMEQ, PASEC) produces score-equivalence claims that may not hold in practice — particularly for sub-Saharan African countries that anchor through small overlapping samples — is engaged head-on in two places: the within-country fixed-effects specification (Model 2) absorbs any time-invariant cross-country level miscalibration in the harmonization, and the AAP-2018 alternative serves as the published-measure check against measurement-choice fragility. Learning-Adjusted Years of Schooling (`hci_lays_overall`, computed by the World Bank as $\text{LAYS} = \text{EYS} \times (\text{HLO}/625)$) is reported as a parallel outcome to put the paper's findings in the unit Angrist [-@angrist2024lays] and the GEEAP [-@geeap2023smart] cost-effectiveness benchmarks use.

The treatment variable is OECD DAC Creditor Reporting System (CRS) disbursements to education (sector codes 110/111/112/113/114), constant USD with the DAC deflator, and a three-year strictly-past moving average (mean of *t*−3, *t*−2, *t*−1). ADR-0005 locks this construction — `crs_disburse_usd_defl_ma3_lag1` — from a 16-cell sensitivity surface that tests commitment-vs-disbursement, current-vs-constant USD, and four lag/MA combinations. All sixteen cells produce a non-negative within-country coefficient on HLO; the strictly-past MA is chosen as primary because it forecloses contemporaneous donor response to within-year learning shocks. The raw OECD CRS extract is a 537,586-row project-level parquet (release CRS-Parquet-v20260408) fetched via the OECD's SDMX endpoint; aggregation to the (iso3, year) panel happens in `R/30_merge_panel.R` at Phase 2. NA cells within the ODA-eligible universe are coalesced to zero before MA computation, on the rationale that ODA-eligible recipients with no recorded CRS project in year *t* received zero dollars that year, not "data missing". AidData's Global Chinese Development Finance v3.0 (GCDF; ADR-0008) is ingested in parallel for the non-DAC blind-spot robustness reported in Appendix B.

Macro and sector controls (WDI: GDP per capita in constant USD; pupil-teacher ratio at primary level; education expenditure as percent of GDP) are fetched via the `WDI` R package. Governance controls use the native Worldwide Governance Indicators bundle from `info.worldbank.org/governance/wgi/` — not the WDI mirror — to retain the per-source count needed to engage Langbein and Knack's [-@langbein2010governance] critique that the six WGI dimensions collapse to a single latent factor and the published aggregates over-state their independence. ADR-0009 locks the operationalization as the PCA-collapsed first principal component (`wgi_pc1`), computed via `prcomp(scale. = TRUE)` on the six WGI estimate columns and sign-flipped to align with the positive governance-quality direction. Empirically, PC1 captures 76.4 % of WGI variance with all six loadings positive in the 0.35–0.45 band; the all-six specification shows none of the six dimensions individually significant despite joint significance, confirming the Langbein-Knack aggregation critique on this sample. ADR-0006 drops UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) variables from the primary specification because the private-expenditure share is 91.8 % missing in sub-Saharan Africa (vs 80.3 % in the rest of the world); a UIS-augmented listwise robustness is reported in Appendix B. The enrollment and out-of-school indicators flowing through WDI and UIS ultimately rest on country-side reporting to UNESCO's annual education survey; ministries face well-documented incentives to over-report enrollment and under-report out-of-school children during MDG and SDG-4 monitoring cycles, and the paper treats these variables as suggestive rather than authoritative measures of schooling participation. The §5 limits paragraph owns this measurement caveat directly.

Two confounder sources control for time-varying disruption. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program / PRIO Armed Conflict Dataset (v25.1 + Battle-Related Deaths v25.1) provides a binary `in_conflict` indicator and intensity counts, aggregated to country-year from the original conflict-level data; 12.3 % of country-year cells in the panel show active conflict, with the expected sub-Saharan over-representation (25.3 % SSA vs 9.2 % rest-of-world). The UNESCO COVID-19 School Closures dataset gives `days_closed` per country-year for 2020–2022, derived transparently from the daily status time series rather than from UNESCO's pre-aggregated figures; cross-validation against the pre-aggregated source agrees at median |diff| = 2 days. Both confounders enter Model 2 as time-varying controls and are documented at variable-level in Appendix C.

## 3.2 Pre-commitment design

The path-c framing the paper foregrounds rests on a design choice the cross-country aid-effectiveness literature has not historically made: every consequential analytical decision is locked in writing in an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) *before* the analysis whose result the decision would influence runs. Twelve ADRs have been written over the project's eleven-month lifespan, and they form the spine of the methodological audit trail Pass 1 verified at Phase 10. The roster: ADR-0001 (toolchain — R + renv + a CLAUDE.md + per-session-log + ADR-continuity model); ADR-0002 (country universe, locked as ODA-eligible ∩ ≥1 HLO observation, N = 133); ADR-0003 (year window, locked as 2010–2020 primary with 2000–2022 / 2005–2020 robustness mechanically identical per the Session-09 viability audit); ADR-0004 (HLO measure choice, locked as WB HCI HLOS primary with AAP-2018 robustness *and a pre-specified sign-agreement gate*); ADR-0005 (treatment construction, locked as strictly-past 3-year MA of constant-USD disbursements after a 16-cell sensitivity grid); ADR-0006 (UIS missingness strategy, locked as drop-from-primary after a Little MCAR test rejected at p ≪ 10⁻⁶); ADR-0007 (CRS intervention typology, **Rejected** because the pre-committed inter-method agreement gate failed on all three criteria — the protocol caught an unfeasible design before it produced defensible-looking but fragile results); ADR-0008 (Chinese-aid robustness, AidData GCDF reported alongside OECD CRS); ADR-0009 (WGI operationalization, PCA-collapsed PC1 primary with Langbein-Knack engagement); ADR-0010 (identification limit, static FE remains headline because System GMM failed Hansen overid at p = 0.022 and the small-T HCI-cycle panel is below the Bond 2002 minimum of T ≥ 5–10); ADR-0011 (Model 5 counterfactual specification, within-support % shocks on the locked aggregate β with plug-in CI propagation); and ADR-0012 (retirement of the UIS multiple-imputation sub-commitment of ADR-0006, because MCAR-rejection makes the MI MAR assumption empirically indefensible). The ADR architecture is not paperwork — it is the operational frame for treating every potentially-arbitrary methodological choice as a falsifiable gate the data must clear.

A second pre-commitment layer wraps the ADR discipline: the brief's Three-Pass Self-Review Protocol. Pass 1 (Statistical Validity) requires running every diagnostic committed to in the project's `obligations.md` before any manuscript writing begins; results are documented privately, and the paper does not proceed until the audit is complete. Pass 2 (Argumentative Coherence) is read-only on Abstract → Introduction → Discussion → Conclusion after the full draft exists, with the question *does the argument hold without the numbers?* Pass 3 (Adversarial Read) follows a deliberate 48-hour gap from the final draft and asks the author to read as a skeptical *World Development* referee, marking every sentence the form *"claim X but did not demonstrate X"* for repair or reframe. Pass 1 closed at Phase 10 as a *qualified pass*: every Statistical-Layer diagnostic is run or documented as not-feasible at our T (the small-T limit forecloses the Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger test by the same data-shape constraint that limits the GMM exercise per ADR-0010), and the principal HLO measure-sensitivity check produced a sign-flip the manuscript now adapts to throughout. Passes 2 and 3 are scheduled for Phases 12 and 13.

The third layer of the pre-commitment design is `obligations.md` — the project's running ledger of every diagnostic test, robustness specification, and reproducibility commitment the manuscript makes. Each item names the obligation, the phase committed to running it, the evidence pointer when complete, and an explicit status marker (`[x]` complete; `[~]` partial; `[N/A]` documented as not-applicable; struck-through with rationale for items withdrawn via an ADR amendment). Twenty-four obligations are checked complete; two are withdrawn per ADR-0007's Rejected status; two are scope-resolved by the Phase-2 reframe of the original 3-level HLM specification to the operative 2-level country-RE + year-FE form; the Granger test is documented as not feasible at our T; Pass 2 / Pass 3 / OSF deposit / `renv::restore` reproducibility checks are deferred to Phases 12, 13, and 14 with documentation. The collective discipline is straightforward: every claim the manuscript makes is traceable to a committed-in-advance diagnostic with documented status, and every methodological choice is locked in an ADR before the result that depends on it is generated.

## 3.4 Pass 1 statistical-validity sign-off

Pass 1 closed as a *qualified pass* at Phase 10 Session 01. Every diagnostic in the brief's Statistical Layer is either executed and passed (eight of ten Model Diagnostics; the relevant Data Integrity items), withdrawn per a documented ADR (the two ANOVA diagnostics now obsolete under ADR-0007 Rejected), passed on documented scope-resolution (the original brief's three-level multilevel-ICC and HLM-convergence items, reframed to country-level-only when the 3-level student-school-country specification was deferred for lack of PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS micro-data), deferred to a later pass with explicit documentation (the causal-language audit to Pass 2 at Phase 12; reproducibility checks to Phase 14), or documented as not feasible at the project's effective time-series length (the Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger test, which requires T > 5 + 3·order = 8 per country and is therefore not estimable on the HCI-cycle panel — the same small-T limit that constrained the System GMM exercise per ADR-0010).

The substantive Pass 1 finding is not the obligations-bookkeeping completion. It is the failed HLO measure-sensitivity check: the principal robustness committed in ADR-0004 — refit Model 2's headline specification on the AAP-2018 alternative outcome and verify sign agreement with the World Bank HCI HLOS specification — produced a sign-flip on both the full AAP coverage (β = −16.67, p = 0.009) and the overlap window restricted to year ≥ 2010 (β = −3.94, p = 0.66). The overlap-window null rules out sample-window composition as the sole driver; the harmonized-measure choice itself materially shapes the headline. ADR-0004 carries the "Data observed (Phase 10 Session 01)" block documenting the failure; the manuscript adapts via the hedge route — the within-country positive headline is reported throughout the paper with explicit measure-qualification ("*in the WB HCI HLOS specification on the 2010–2020 panel*") rather than naked attribution. §4.7 reports the sensitivity numbers; §5 frames the measure-fragility as itself a methodological contribution to the cross-country aid-learning literature, alongside the Model 4 drop (§4.4 / ADR-0007 Rejected) and the UIS multiple-imputation retirement (§4.7 / ADR-0012).

# 4. Results

## 4.1 Descriptive: Enrollment-learning divergence

The analytical universe is the 133-country sample locked in §3.1 (ODA-eligible countries with at least one HLO observation in 2000–2022, per ADR-0002), with the primary window narrowed to 2010–2020 per ADR-0003. The HLO outcome is observed only in four Human Capital Index assessment cycles (2010, 2017, 2018, 2020), and within-country variation is therefore identified off at most four observations per country — a structural feature of the harmonized cross-country learning measurement landscape that constrains every downstream identification claim. Of the 133-country universe, 127 countries have at least two HLO observations and are within-country fixed-effects identifiable; 30 of the 133 (23 percent) eventually drop out of Model 2 via listwise on controls plus singleton-FE absorption.

<!--
EVIDENCE TRACE — §4.1 ¶1 (sample + period):
- 133-country ADR-0002 universe + 127 FE-identifiable → docs/findings.md §4.1 ¶1

- Cross-reference to manuscript §3.1 (data sources)
- N=143 / 30-country drop → docs/findings.md §5.2 limits paragraph
- Hedge level: LOW (all numbers from project-internal authored sources)
-->

The descriptive headline of the panel is the divergence between enrollment and learning. Gross primary enrollment is uniformly high across all six World Bank regions over the primary window — region means range from 98.5 percent (Europe & Central Asia) to 109.1 percent (Latin America & Caribbean). HLO score is not: the same six-region grid spans 82 points (sub-Saharan Africa 374; ECA 456), roughly 1.6 within-universe standard deviations. The harmonized LAYS measure shows a 4.3-year cross-region spread (SSA 4.9; ECA 9.2). On the 2020 cross-section — the densest cycle, with 106 countries reporting both indicators — the bivariate OLS slope of HLO on gross primary enrollment is **−0.65 HLO points per one-percentage-point enrollment increase** (p = 0.13, not significant); the R² is 0.02. Enrollment "explains" approximately two percent of cross-country HLO variance, and the relationship is trending slightly negative. The named-country contrast that grounds the abstraction: **Kenya** enrolls 92 percent of primary-aged students gross and produces an HLO score of 455; **Bangladesh** enrolls 110 percent gross and produces an HLO score of 368. Bangladesh has eighteen percentage points more gross enrollment than Kenya and an eighty-seven-point lower HLO score, in the same year, on the same harmonized scale.

The regional pattern depth confirms the cross-country selection problem Model 1 will recover empirically and Model 2 will then attempt to escape. Sub-Saharan Africa carries the heaviest aggregate burden: lowest HLO score (374), lowest LAYS (4.9 years), highest pupil-teacher ratio in primary (40.6, against ECA's 16.4), worst primary completion rate (70 percent, against ECA's 97 percent), highest primary out-of-school rate (18.6 percent), and lowest WGI government effectiveness (−0.79, against ECA's −0.14). Europe & Central Asia is the high-functioning low-aid comparator at the other end of every gradient. South Asia, with only seven countries in the universe, carries the heaviest concentrated aid burden — $349 million per country-year in OECD CRS education disbursements (against the panel mean of $96 million), dominated by India — and the longest COVID-19 school closures in 2020 (179 days, against East Asia & Pacific's 73). The variables that vary cross-sectionally with HLO score are precisely the variables that also vary cross-sectionally with aid intensity; this is the structural confounding the within-country fixed-effects specification of §4.2 ¶2 is designed to absorb.

## 4.2 Models 1 & 2: The cross-section vs within-country contrast

Model 1 estimates the cross-sectional ordinary least squares association between ODA intensity and learning outcomes at the country level, using country-mean values over the primary 2010–2020 window. The full universe of 133 countries shrinks to 120 in the full specification once the listwise constraint on the four structural controls (log GDP per capita, primary pupil-teacher ratio, government education expenditure as a share of GDP, and WGI Government Effectiveness) is imposed. The bivariate slope on log(1 + country-mean OECD CRS education disbursement, constant USD) is **β = −11.54** (HC-robust SE 2.72; p < 0.001) — the classical cross-sectional pattern in which aid concentrates in countries with poor outcomes, and would look alarming if reported as the headline. Adding log GDP per capita absorbs approximately ninety percent of the bivariate coefficient (β = −1.20, not significant); each subsequent control leaves the ODA coefficient essentially at zero. The full specification 1e returns **β = −1.36** (SE 2.48; p = 0.584; N = 120; R² = 0.444). The dominant cross-sectional correlate of HLO in this specification is WGI Government Effectiveness, at β = +24.5 HLO points per one-unit WGI improvement (p < 0.01) — roughly half a within-universe standard deviation per unit of governance quality. The substantive read of Model 1 is straightforward: the cross-sectional negative association between aid and learning is selection-driven, and once the structural confounders the literature has long identified as the binding cross-country correlates of learning are absorbed, aid intensity has no cross-sectional association with learning outcomes at all.

Model 2 re-estimates the ODA-on-HLO relationship as a within-country fixed-effects panel on the same universe, exploiting variation across the four HCI-cycle observations per country rather than across-country differences in country-mean values. The specification is two-way (country plus year) fixed effects, country-clustered standard errors, with the post-Phase-5 locked encoding stack: the ODA treatment is the three-year strictly-past moving average of disbursements in constant USD (`crs_disburse_usd_defl_ma3_lag1`), locked in ADR-0005 to foreclose contemporaneous donor response to in-year learning shocks; the governance control is the principal component PC1 of all six WGI dimensions, locked in ADR-0009 to engage the Langbein and Knack (2010) critique that the six WGI aggregates are not empirically separable (PC1 captures 76.4 percent of variance on this sample); and the parallel Chinese-aid covariate in robustness specification 2f is the strictly-past three-year moving average of AidData GCDF education flows, methodologically consistent with the ODA encoding per ADR-0008. The headline specification is 2e, which returns **β = +11.14** HLO points per unit log treatment (SE 5.52; p = 0.048; N = 143), **in the WB HCI HLOS specification on the 2010–2020 panel** — the long-form hedge that the §4.7 measure-sensitivity check (refit on the published Altinok-Angrist-Patrinos 2018 alternative HLO measure) does not survive sign-agreement. The contrast against Model 1 is the manuscript's central empirical claim: cross-sectional **β = −1.36 not significant** absorbs to a near-zero null on observables, while within-country **β = +11.14 significant** at the conventional 0.05 threshold — a sign-flip plus an approximately eight-fold magnitude shift under the within-country specification. The spec progression on the locked encoding shows where the within-country signal emerges: at 2a and 2b (bivariate and with log GDP per capita only) the coefficient is essentially zero and not significant; at 2c, once the time-varying pupil-teacher ratio is added as a control, it rises to β = 9.72 (p = 0.054); at 2e, the headline, it tightens to β = 11.14 (p = 0.048); at 2f, with parallel Chinese aid added, it holds at β = 11.26 (p = 0.046); and at 2g, with active-conflict status and COVID-19 closure days added, it softens to marginal at β = 9.61 (p = 0.082). The robustness across the controlled spec progression is the cleanest within-spec evidence for the headline.

The substantive read of the sign-flip plus magnitude story is consequential but bounded. In the principal specification, a country that moves from roughly $10 million to $100 million in average annual education disbursement (a log change of approximately 2.3) would experience a within-country HLO score gain of about twenty-six points — roughly half a within-universe standard deviation. The reading is not causal in the structural-causal sense that within-country fixed effects absorb time-invariant country-quality confounding but do not rule out time-varying endogeneity. Donors may target countries with rising learning trajectories — the lagged-dependent-variable "donor success-chasing" channel — and the static-FE specification cannot distinguish between aid that produces learning and aid that follows it. This is the limit owned in §4.3 (Model 3, the multilevel transparency counterpart that recovers Model 1's cross-sectional null and thereby validates the within-FE specification's identification logic via Hausman) and re-engaged in the §6 limits paragraph. What within-FE *does* rule out is the standard cross-country-confounding story that Model 1 makes visible: in the principal specification, the conditional-on-observables association between within-country variation in ODA and within-country variation in HLO is positive and meaningful in magnitude, not absorbed by income, by the pupil-teacher ratio, by education expenditure shares, or by the broader WGI governance composite. The headline-specification diagnostics are clean: the Wooldridge AR(1) test returns F = 0.44 (p = 0.51, no serial autocorrelation detected); the Breusch-Pagan test rejects homoskedasticity at χ² = 137 (p = 0.0045), and the country-clustered SE adjustment already applied addresses it; and the maximum variance inflation factor on the demeaned regressors is 1.62, with all VIFs below two on the within-transformed specification. The cross-sectional collinearity between governance and income — a binding identification concern for Model 1, where the WGI and log GDP per capita correlate at r = 0.79 — is fully absorbed by the within-country demeaning, which is the FE specification's hidden virtue.

The qualifications on the headline are real and shape every reading of it. N = 143 is thin: thirty of the 133 universe countries (23 percent) drop via the combined listwise constraint on the four controls plus singleton-FE absorption when within-country variation is not identifiable. HCI cycle sparsity — the four observations are concentrated in 2010, 2017, 2018, and 2020, with the bulk of within-country variation identified off two or three cycles per country — makes this a small-T panel, in which asymptotic standard errors may understate the true sampling uncertainty. Reverse causality, as noted above, is not ruled out by the static-FE specification, and the System GMM remedy committed in [ADR-0010](../docs/decisions/0010-identification-strategy-gmm.md) is not feasible on this panel because T_eff ≤ 4 lies far below the GMM-identification threshold (this is the same small-T limit that the Dumitrescu-Hurlin Granger pre-test of §3.4 also cannot clear). And — most consequentially — the within-country positive coefficient does not survive the principal robustness check committed in [ADR-0004](../docs/decisions/0004-hlo-measure.md): refitting Model 2's headline specification on the published Altinok-Angrist-Patrinos (2018) [@altinok2018global] alternative HLO measure reverses the sign on both the full AAP coverage window (β = −16.67; SE 5.96; p = 0.009; N = 69 on 1995–2015) and the overlap window restricted to year ≥ 2010 (β = −3.94; SE 8.68; p = 0.66; N = 36). The overlap-window null rules out sample-window composition as the sole driver of the sign-flip; the harmonized-measure choice itself materially shapes the within-country answer. §4.7 reports the AAP-2018 sensitivity in full alongside the UIS-augmented listwise check that the missingness ADR also pre-committed to. §5 then frames the measure-fragility as itself a methodological contribution to the cross-country aid-learning literature — alongside the typology-axis non-recovery of §4.4 (Model 4 dropped per ADR-0007) and the multiple-imputation retirement of [ADR-0012](../docs/decisions/0012-retirement-of-uis-multiple-imputation.md). The hedge that runs throughout the manuscript reflects this discipline rather than rhetorical caution: the within-country positive coefficient is real in the principal specification, on the principal sample window, and the published-measure alternative reverses it.

# 5. Discussion — Why the system perpetuates itself

## 5.1 Thesis

Three findings, taken together, mark out the empirical terrain of cross-country aid-effectiveness research as more constrained than the standard literature has admitted. *First*, the four-bucket intervention typology the policy literature [@glewwe2016improving; @geeap2023smart] treats as the operative axis of "what aid composition produces learning" is not recoverable from the standard donor-reporting dataset (OECD CRS project metadata) at any inter-method agreement threshold a referee would accept; the typology-ANOVA the brief and the field both expected from this kind of panel cannot be defensibly produced. *Second*, the within-country positive aid-to-learning coefficient that the cross-country panel evidence does identify (β = +11.14 HLO points; p ≈ 0.05) is sensitive to the choice of harmonized learning measurement: the published Altinok-Angrist-Patrinos (2018) alternative reverses the sign in both the full AAP coverage window and the overlap window restricted to 2010 onward — the headline is real in one specification but does not carry across the published-measure choice. *Third*, the multiple-imputation robustness check the missingness ADR pre-committed to requires assumptions (MAR) the MCAR test the same ADR pre-committed to running already refutes; the standard sensitivity-direction the literature treats as default is not, on this data, empirically defensible. Alongside, the paper's HCI × AI-readiness joint composite quantifies a previously unmeasured ≈2× sub-Saharan-African over-representation in the low-HCI ∩ low-AI-readiness cell, giving the qualitative compounding-divergence thesis a concrete cross-section. *What the cross-country aid-effectiveness panel literature can rigorously claim from data at this shape is narrower than the policy discourse has been treating it as. The paper's principal contribution is mapping that narrower terrain precisely, with the pre-commitment apparatus visible enough that the next paper attempting similar work knows which choices the field needs to make differently.*
